summary_of_pdf: A formal pre-litigation demand letter and notice of potential infringement sent by Reinaldo J. Aguiar Marcano to the General Counsel of Amazon.com, Inc. The correspondence asserts that Amazon's logistics network, delivery vehicles, and a specific retail location in New York City potentially infringe six pending U.S. patent applications related to covert communications, supply chain manipulation, and encryption. The sender seeks to establish actual notice of the published applications to preserve provisional rights under 35 U.S.C. § 154(d) and proposes a licensing arrangement conditioned upon Amazon publicly marking its vehicles and stores with the application numbers or inventor's name.
attorneys_comments: Upon careful evidentiary review, this correspondence presents as a highly speculative pre-litigation demand aimed at establishing actual notice under 35 U.S.C. § 154(d) to accrue potential reasonable royalty damages from the date of application publication. Tactically, the claimant is attempting to lay the groundwork for future litigation upon the issuance of any patents. However, the evidentiary strength of the infringement allegations is exceedingly weak; the claimant provides no claim charts or substantive mapping of Amazon's operations to the pending claims. Furthermore, the subject matter of the applications (e.g., 'covert communication using arrangements of satellite-observable, distinctively colored objects') raises immediate red flags for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice Corp.). The proposed licensing condition—requiring Amazon to cover 3% of its delivery vehicles and store signage with patent markings—is commercially absurd and strongly suggests the sender lacks sophisticated patent counsel. Procedurally, because no patents have issued, there is no immediate threat of an injunction or actionable infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271. Any future litigation would likely face strict venue scrutiny under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) and TC Heartland, despite the sender's Texas domicile.
recommended_next_steps: 1. Acknowledge receipt of the correspondence in writing without admitting any liability, validity, or enforceability of the referenced applications. 2. Forward the six USPTO application numbers to outside patent prosecution counsel to monitor the file wrappers for office actions, claim amendments, and potential issuance. 3. Conduct a preliminary 35 U.S.C. § 101 and prior art assessment on the published claims to prepare defensive invalidity positions. 4. Do not engage in substantive licensing negotiations or agree to any marking demands, as no enforceable patent rights currently exist. 5. Institute a routine, narrowly tailored document preservation hold regarding the specific Brookfield Place store operations and logistics tracking systems mentioned, purely out of an abundance of caution.
